title: Cognitive biases
description: Name the common errors of judgment and spot them in everyday decisions.

ideas.title: Two systems and heuristics
ideas.summary: Fast intuitive thinking runs on shortcuts that usually work and sometimes fail in predictable ways.

items.q: In Daniel Kahneman's "Thinking, Fast and Slow", what is System 1?
items.a: Fast, automatic, intuitive thinking

items.q: In Daniel Kahneman's "Thinking, Fast and Slow", what is System 2?
items.a: Slow, effortful, deliberate thinking

items.q: In the psychology of judgment, what is a heuristic?
items.a: A mental shortcut that gives a quick answer that is usually good enough

items.q: Which two psychologists launched the study of heuristics and biases in the 1970s?
items.a: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky

ideas.title: Reference points and wording
ideas.summary: The first number we hear and the way a choice is worded shift our judgment more than they should.

items.q: What is the anchoring effect?
items.a: Estimates are pulled toward the first number we encounter, even an irrelevant one

items.q: A shop lists a $900 jacket first so the $300 one feels cheap. Which bias is it relying on?
items.a: Anchoring

items.q: What is the framing effect?
items.a: The same facts lead to different choices depending on how they are presented

items.q: Shoppers rate beef labeled "75% lean" more highly than the same beef labeled "25% fat". Which effect is this?
items.a: The framing effect

ideas.title: Availability and base rates
ideas.summary: We judge likelihood by the examples that come to mind, and overlook how common a thing really is and what we never see.

items.q: What is the availability heuristic?
items.a: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind

items.q: After news of a plane crash, people overestimate the danger of flying. Which heuristic explains this?
items.a: The availability heuristic

items.q: What is base rate neglect?
items.a: Ignoring how common something is in general and judging only from the details of the case

items.q: What is the gambler's fallacy?
items.a: Believing that a run of one outcome makes the opposite due, when each event is independent

items.q: Studying bombers that returned from wartime missions, Abraham Wald advised armoring the places with no bullet holes. Which bias was he avoiding?
items.a: Survivorship bias

ideas.title: Confirmation and overconfidence
ideas.summary: We look for evidence that we are right, feel afterwards that we knew it all along, and trust our forecasts too much.

items.q: What is confirmation bias?
items.a: The tendency to seek, notice and remember evidence that supports what we already believe

items.q: After his team loses, a fan who predicted a win says the defeat was obvious all along. Which bias is this?
items.a: Hindsight bias

items.q: Which fallacy, named by Kahneman and Tversky, is underestimating how long your own project will take?
items.a: The planning fallacy

items.q: What does it mean for a person's judgments to be well calibrated?
items.a: Their confidence matches their accuracy: of the things they call 80% likely, about 80% happen

ideas.title: Loss aversion and sunk costs
ideas.summary: Losses hurt more than equal gains please, so we cling to what we have and to what we have already spent.

items.q: What is loss aversion?
items.a: Losing something hurts more than gaining the same thing pleases, often put at about twice as much

items.q: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
items.a: Carrying on with something because of what you have already spent, though that cost cannot be recovered

items.q: What is the endowment effect?
items.a: Valuing something more highly simply because you own it

items.q: You sit through a film you dislike because you paid for the ticket. Which fallacy is this?
items.a: The sunk cost fallacy

ideas.title: Judging other people
ideas.summary: We explain other people's behavior by their character rather than their situation, and let one trait color the rest.

items.q: What is the fundamental attribution error?
items.a: Explaining other people's behavior by their character while underrating the situation they are in

items.q: What is the halo effect?
items.a: One good trait, such as attractiveness, colors our judgment of a person's other qualities

items.q: A driver cuts in front of you and you think "what a selfish person", not "perhaps there is an emergency". Which error is this?
items.a: The fundamental attribution error
